theme: The call is the ritual, not what gets said on it. A week about the short calls, the missed ones, and letting a normal day be enough without needing to ask about it every time.

posts.text: The call still goes short: hi, how are you, good, you? Fine. Okay, talk soon. For years I thought that meant we weren't saying the real things. Now I think the real thing was that the call happened at all.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic strip: an adult son calls his mother from a train, she answers from her kitchen saying she is watering the tomatoes, he hangs up at the platform looking at ease. Caption: That was the whole call. It was enough.

posts.title: Three questions that open a call, not an inspection
posts.text:
Three questions that open a call, not an inspection

A short daily call goes further with a plain question than with "are you okay?" These three keep the answer easy and the tone warm, for anyone who calls a parent from far away.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic strip: a mother gardening, having tea with a crossword, and reading by the window, each captioned with a simple question to open a call: What's growing this week, What did you have for lunch, Tell me something boring that happened today.
posts.note: Self-check (copy): no banned words, no verdict, no em dash, no kinship/culture words, no medical claim, no invented stat, June shown capable and busy, no CTA. Image: failed after 2 regenerations (3 attempts) - the model could not render the quoted captions cleanly (garbled letters) and one attempt drew Sam instead of June in panel 1 plus an unspecified speech bubble. posts.title: The calls we keep missing

script.say: My parents are twelve hours away. When it's morning for me, it's already night for them. We used to play phone tag for days.
script.broll: Founder face to camera, kitchen counter behind him, phone visible face down on the counter.

script.say: I stopped needing the call to tell me her morning was fine. I just wanted to know it had happened, even on the days we never managed to talk.
script.overlay: I just wanted to know it happened
script.broll: Founder face to camera, phone in hand, thoughtful pause.

script.say: So I built Kettle. It notices when Mom's normal morning happens, on the phone she already carries, and tells our family in a short note, twice a day.
script.overlay: Notices her normal morning. Twice a day.
script.broll: Neutral b-roll: a plain phone face up on a kitchen table, no app visible, morning light.

script.say: Some days we still miss each other's calls. That's all right now. I already know she's had her tea.
script.overlay: We still miss the calls. That's all right now.
script.broll: Founder face to camera, small smile, kettle visible on the counter behind him.

posts.text: We keep missing each other's calls.

posts.title: Right on time

script.say: Some mornings the phone actually rings when I expect it. Mom, right on time, telling me about the crossword.
script.broll: Founder face to camera, warm kitchen light.

script.say: Most mornings it doesn't ring at all, and that used to worry me more than it should have. I didn't want to call and check on her. I wanted to know her morning had already happened, on its own.
script.overlay: I wanted to know it already happened

script.say: Kettle notices when Mom's normal morning happens, using the phone she already carries, and sends our family a short note, twice a day.
script.overlay: A short note. Twice a day.
script.broll: Neutral b-roll: a plain phone face up on a kitchen table, no app visible, morning light.

posts.text: The call was never really about what got said. It was about it happening at all: the phone ringing, her voice, mine. Everything else was just talk.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic strip: a phone lights up on a desk, a mother answers at her kitchen table with a kettle steaming behind her. Caption: It happened. That was the whole point.
